youtube.title: Who Owns Gibraltar? The 6.8 km² Rock Spain Has Wanted for 313 Years
youtube.description:
Who owns Gibraltar? Britain has held the Rock of Gibraltar since the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, yet Spain has never accepted British rule. Gibraltar's history takes in the Great Siege, a border closed from 1969 to 1985, two referendums, Brexit and the 2025 deal on the land border. So why can't Spain get Gibraltar back?

On the map we follow the strait that around 100,000 ships a year pass through, the treaty lines of 1713, the Great Siege, the disputed sand under the airport, the closed border of 1969 to 1985, two referendums, Brexit and the 2025 deal on the land border. Both sides' cases are given in full, with sources for every figure.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: Gibraltar's area is about 6.8 square kilometres and grows with land reclamation
sources.source: HM Government of Gibraltar / Gibraltar Tourist Board, 'About Gibraltar' (2024)

sources.claim: Britain has held Gibraltar since 1713 (313 years in 2026)
sources.source: Treaty of Utrecht between Spain and Great Britain, 13 July 1713, Article X

sources.claim: Around 100,000 ships a year pass through the Strait of Gibraltar, tracked from Tarifa
sources.source: Salvamento Marítimo (Spanish Maritime Safety Agency), Tarifa Traffic Centre annual figures

sources.claim: Ships between Asia and northern Europe via the Suez Canal leave the Mediterranean through the Strait of Gibraltar
sources.source: UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport (2024): Asia-Europe route via Suez

sources.claim: Gibraltar is a peninsula about 5 km long joined to Spain by a sandy isthmus
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gibraltar' (about 3 miles / 5 km long)

sources.claim: 32,194 people lived in Gibraltar at the 2012 census, its last full census
sources.source: Gibraltar Statistics Office, Census of Gibraltar 2012

sources.claim: Algeciras is about 9 km west across the bay
sources.source: Measured on the map, Gibraltar town to Algeciras port

sources.claim: Algeciras handled over 4.5 million container units (TEU) in 2023
sources.source: Puertos del Estado, Estadísticas portuarias 2023; Port of Algeciras Bay Authority annual report 2023

sources.claim: The strait is about 14 km wide at its narrowest; Britannica gives 13 km
sources.source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Strait of Gibraltar' (about 14 km); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Strait of Gibraltar' (8 miles / 13 km)

sources.claim: The Camarinal Sill lies about 280 metres down
sources.source: Armi & Farmer, 'The flow of Mediterranean water through the Strait of Gibraltar', Progress in Oceanography 21 (1988): sill depth about 284 m

sources.claim: Britain keeps a naval base on Gibraltar used by its warships and submarines
sources.source: UK Ministry of Defence, British Forces Gibraltar (2024)

sources.claim: A road tunnel under the runway opened in 2023; pedestrians and cyclists still cross the runway
sources.source: HM Government of Gibraltar press release on the opening of the Kingsway tunnel, 31 March 2023

sources.claim: Around 15,000 workers cross the land border on a working day
sources.source: House of Commons Library, 'Gibraltar and Brexit' briefing (2021, updated 2023)

sources.claim: La Línea, San Roque and Algeciras are Spanish towns of the Campo de Gibraltar around the bay
sources.source: Mancomunidad de Municipios del Campo de Gibraltar, member municipalities

sources.claim: Spain says the isthmus was never ceded in 1713
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 'La Cuestión de Gibraltar' (2008)

sources.claim: King Charles II of Spain died childless in 1700, starting the War of the Spanish Succession
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'War of the Spanish Succession'

sources.claim: An English and Dutch fleet took Gibraltar on 4 August 1704 in the name of Archduke Charles
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gibraltar: History'; William Jackson, 'The Rock of the Gibraltarians' (1987)

sources.claim: Most Spanish residents left; many settled in San Roque, about 8 km north, whose title says the city of Gibraltar resides there
sources.source: Ayuntamiento de San Roque, official title 'donde reside la de Gibraltar'; Jackson (1987)

sources.claim: Britain and Spain made peace at Utrecht on 13 July 1713; Article X yields town, castle, port and fortifications 'for ever', 'without any territorial jurisdiction' and 'without any open communication by land', with Spain given first refusal
sources.source: Treaty of Peace and Friendship between Great Britain and Spain, Utrecht, 13 July 1713, Article X

sources.claim: Spain besieged Gibraltar in 1727 and failed within months; the 1713 line stayed
sources.source: Jackson, 'The Rock of the Gibraltarians' (1987): siege February-June 1727

sources.claim: Spain built a fortified line across the isthmus in the 1730s, leaving neutral ground
sources.source: Jackson (1987); Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2008)

sources.claim: The Great Siege lasted from 1779 to 1783; French forces joined the effort later, mainly from 1782; tunnels began in 1782
sources.source: Gibraltar Heritage Trust, Great Siege Tunnels; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Great Siege of Gibraltar'

sources.claim: The 1783 peace left Gibraltar British, its line unchanged
sources.source: Treaty of Versailles between Great Britain and Spain, 3 September 1783

sources.claim: In 1815, during a yellow fever outbreak, Britain set up camps on the neutral ground; Spain says only temporarily
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 'La Cuestión de Gibraltar' (2008); Jackson (1987)

sources.claim: Britain says long use made the land British and built a fence in 1909
sources.source: House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, 'Gibraltar' (HC 461, 2014); Jackson (1987)

sources.claim: The racecourse became an airfield in the Second World War and the runway was extended into the bay with tunnel spoil
sources.source: Gibraltar International Airport, history; Jackson (1987)

sources.claim: Gibraltar was placed on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories in 1946
sources.source: United Nations Special Committee on Decolonization, list of Non-Self-Governing Territories

sources.claim: On 10 September 1967, 12,138 voted to keep the link with Britain and 44 for Spain; the isthmus stayed British-held and disputed by Spain
sources.source: HM Government of Gibraltar, 1967 referendum results; House of Commons Library briefing; Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2008)

sources.claim: The 1969 constitution recorded Britain's promise never to transfer Gibraltar's people against their wishes
sources.source: Gibraltar Constitution Order 1969, preamble

sources.claim: Spain was ruled by General Franco in 1969
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Francisco Franco' (head of state 1939-1975)

sources.claim: Spain closed the land border on 8 June 1969; phone lines were cut and the Algeciras ferry stopped
sources.source: House of Commons Library, 'Gibraltar' briefing; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gibraltar: History'

sources.claim: Pedestrian crossing reopened in December 1982; full reopening in February 1985
sources.source: House of Commons Library, 'Gibraltar' briefing: 15 December 1982 and 5 February 1985

sources.claim: Spain joined the European Community in 1986; Gibraltar had joined with the UK in 1973
sources.source: Treaty of Accession of Spain (1985, in force 1 January 1986); EEC Treaty Article 227(4)

sources.claim: On 23 June 2016 Gibraltar voted 19,322 to Remain and 823 to Leave
sources.source: UK Electoral Commission, EU referendum results 2016

sources.claim: EU leaders agreed in April 2017 that no EU-UK deal would apply to Gibraltar without Spain-UK agreement
sources.source: European Council (Art. 50) guidelines, 29 April 2017, paragraph 24

sources.claim: Spanish governments call Gibraltar the last colony in Europe
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 'La Cuestión de Gibraltar' (2008)

sources.claim: A 1967 UN resolution says colonial situations that break up a country's territory are incompatible with the Charter
sources.source: UN General Assembly Resolution 2353 (XXII), 19 December 1967

sources.claim: Spain says Gibraltar's waters end at the port; Britain claims 3 nautical miles (about 5.5 km)
sources.source: UK Government, British Gibraltar Territorial Waters statements; Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2008)

sources.claim: Spanish and British vessels meet in the waters and each government protests
sources.source: UK Parliament written answers on incursions into British Gibraltar Territorial Waters (2019-2024)

sources.claim: On 7 November 2002, 187 voted for shared sovereignty and 17,900 against
sources.source: HM Government of Gibraltar, referendum results, 7 November 2002

sources.claim: About 99 percent of valid votes rejected shared sovereignty in 2002
sources.source: Our calculation from HM Government of Gibraltar results, 7 November 2002: 17,900 of 18,087 valid votes = 98.97%

sources.claim: Britain and Spain discussed sharing sovereignty in 2001-2002
sources.source: UK Foreign Secretary Jack Straw, statement to the House of Commons, 12 July 2002

sources.claim: Gibraltar's government cites the UN Charter principle of self-determination
sources.source: UN Charter, Article 1(2); HM Government of Gibraltar statements to the UN Fourth Committee

sources.claim: Ceuta is about 25 km south of Gibraltar
sources.source: Measured on the map, Europa Point to Ceuta

sources.claim: Morocco says Ceuta and Melilla should be Moroccan; Spain says they are full parts of Spain
sources.source: Moroccan Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements; Statutes of Autonomy of Ceuta and Melilla (1995)

sources.claim: Portugal took Ceuta in 1415; Spain took Melilla in 1497; Ceuta passed to Spain in 1668
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ceuta' and 'Melilla'; Treaty of Lisbon (1668)

sources.claim: Ceuta and Melilla are not on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories
sources.source: United Nations Special Committee on Decolonization, list of Non-Self-Governing Territories

sources.claim: On 31 December 2020 Spain and the UK agreed a framework for Gibraltar
sources.source: UK Government and Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements, 31 December 2020

sources.claim: On 11 June 2025 the UK, Spain, the EU and Gibraltar announced a political agreement in Brussels
sources.source: European Commission press release, 11 June 2025; UK FCDO statement, 11 June 2025

sources.claim: The deal removes routine land border checks, moves Schengen checks to the port and airport with Spanish officers, creates a customs union and aligns tobacco taxes; both sides keep their sovereignty positions
sources.source: European Commission press release and UK FCDO statement, 11 June 2025

sources.claim: Britain has promised that any change of sovereignty would need the consent of Gibraltar's people
sources.source: Gibraltar Constitution Order 2006, preamble (a UK commitment, not an entrenched legal bar)
